doc.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Mingus's tantrum at the Five Spot and Abbey Lincoln's trio request
summary: While Walton's trio played opposite Mingus, Mingus wrecked his bass in a fit, and Abbey Lincoln told Max Roach this was the trio she wanted to record with.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: One of the things you said you wanted to, to speak on, uh, is your time with Abbey Lincoln.
You were talking about the first rehearsal.

Yeah. Yeah, uh, I think it started when, uh, I told you that uh, I stopped Art Blakey and went into the Five Spot for a long-term engagement and we were opposite, uh, was a trio where we were opposite the Mingus dynasty. I'm not sure he called it the dynasty then, but …

Yeah, and he had uh, sometimes quintets, sometimes sextet, and uh, uh, Max Roach was really fond of uh, of Mingus, especially, you know, he would go see him all the time. And he and Abbey Lincoln who, uh, recently married at that time, came and uh, um, Mingus was having one of his tantrums. In fact, he had his bass by the neck and he was draggin' it through some, uh, goin' toward the stage through some swinging doors. You know, it was just … practically mutilated his bass. He just let 'em close, you know. It was terrible and uh, uh, and he kept uh, sayin' where everybody could hear him, "I'm sorry Max, but you know, I don't mean to be doin' this, and I'm sorry." That's, that's what I remember, you know. And uh, I can't even remember the outcome. But anyway, during that time, that evening, uh, Abbey Lincoln told Max, "Well, this is the trio I'd like to record with." So uh, uh, I think we ended up doin' it, except by that time Tootie
wasn't around. We had a guy named J.C. Moses, uh, who's from Pittsburgh, and we had uh, Reggie, uh, we uh …
